IPT.evidence_source: [/page/4/Text/8] The results of our study suggest that cognitive bibliotherapy may be an effective treatment for adolescents experiencing depressive symptoms

dxgive.evidence_source: [/page/4/Text/10] Finally, the presence of depressive symptoms—and not a diagnosis of major depression or dysthymia—was required for entry into our study, so our results should not be generalized to people with major depression or dysthymia.

Source.evidence_source: [/page/4/Text/9] The failure to find clinically significant change with the CBCL-D raises further questions. Although there were statistically significant changes that indicated a decrease in depressive symptoms, the level of improvement reported by parents was not sufficient to be regarded as clinically meaningful. It is our opinion that the adolescents' self-reports are a more important data source than parent ratings because depressed mood is, after all, primarily a subjective state. [/page/4/Text/11] Dysfunctional attitudes improved with treatment, and there was evidence that this change mediated improvement in depressive symptoms as measured by the CDI but not as measured by the HRSD and the CBCL-D.

MedCat.evidence_source: [/page/4/Text/9] The failure to find clinically significant change with the CBCL-D raises further questions. [/page/4/Text/11] Results from the DAS data, but not the ATQ data, partially supported Beck's (1970) cognitive view of depression. Dysfunctional attitudes improved with treatment, and there was evidence that this change mediated improvement in depressive symptoms as measured by the CDI but not as measured by the HRSD and the CBCL-D.
